reviews.review:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.
There needs to be a season 2

Short game with great plot and character development and interesting ideas.
Well worth playing!

Just finished the first playthrough of this little gem and I got to say it's brilliant in my book.
It's not that long, but it motivates you to see the different endings and try the alternative paths. I can see myself giving the story another go in the near future. 
I really enjoyed it and for 10 bucks (or 25% off while writing this) it gives you a pleasant ride.
I can fully recommend it to you, even more so, if you, like me, have a fable for utopian stories. You'll be sucked in and won't regret it any time soon. The Nation awaits you, investigator!

Loved the concept, enjoyed the game. It's 5 hours long at most, but I would love to play it again in the future and choose differently to see a possible different course of actio.

Different to most visual novels and makes you fell really involved in the story as it unfolds.

Not really any 'gameplay' but it workd perfectly for this type of story. Would love to see more like this or see this story expant with many different outcomes and options.

A quick, delightful game that allowed me to follow a story with some really cool twists and turns. It's taken me about 3-4 hours to go through it once and I can't wait to play it again! What if I had made different choices? What if I hadn't acted at certain points? The game mechanics mean that inaction is just as much of a choice as action and that's COOL. Games that make you want to replay them as soon as you finish? Fantastic.
Orwell is a fun game for a really good price. The writing is good and the art is pleasant.
It's not a super complex sherlock holmes game, but it has its depths in other places.
Lends to an entertaining evening!
Quite the intriguing game. I'm only about an hour and a half in, but that hour and a half flew by as I became an agent of the state.
This game was top of the line. Roller Coaster from start to finish. Would love a sequel or a second story. worth double the price personaly.
A good game not unlike papers please. It has a strong story and good paceing and is only held back by being a bit to short.

This game is really good. I'm really impressed. I was afraid it would be too formulaic and that the game would be making all of the important decisions for you, but there are enough real choices to make, with actual ways to figure out what the "right" choice is, that this game is super satisfying. If you've played Her Story or games in that same vein, you'll like this game, too. There's lots of threads to tug and the game rewards you for paying closer attention than just reading what it automatically highlights for you. If you're a weirdo like me who really enjoys research, this game is for you. It's detailed, the story is great, the grahpics and interface and engaging.

The only negative? It's kind of short. Each "episode" lasts about an hour and there are five episodes. But that said, it's still more than worth the money. I just wish it went on longer because I was enjoying it so much. I didn't feel jipped by the length, is what I mean.

Amazingggg. you play as a big brother type character in this society controlled by the government, at first i thought it was a simple story abotu a woman named cassandra. nope. cassandra was just one part of something huge.  every plot twist had me at the edge of my seat, i stayed up for hours on end playing! i really reccomend this if your into plot twists, story based games, and great sound effects.

Play as an investigator in a new secret gov. program named 'Orwell' that -- unsurprisingly -- spies on its own citizens' e-mails, phone conversations, laptops, etc., and selectively hunts for evidence of unlawful activity. The focus in this 5-part story is anti-governmental terrorism.

The name Orwell is on the nose, of course, and the writing is mostly along those lines. (This game is all text, all writing, so this is very important!) It, however, begins unraveling near the end, reaching for genuine philosophical depth. A favorite moment that's a bit too prescient is at the end while digging through the (optional) files that led to Orwell's creation. One of the creators calls the program Orwellian in its sinister direction. It's meant as a pejorative. The other creators have no idea who Orwell is -- one of the most famous English writers of the 20th century, and most influential on pop culture for over 50 years. They just think Orwell is a cool name, and so they use it unironically to name their entire Orwellian program. 

Do you see what's neat here?

I went in thinking Orwell didn't exist in this game's universe. But he does. And he's still a huge influence. The fictional government is so ignorant, run by idiots hell-bent on imaginary terrorism and protecting themselves and their interests, though, that the messages of Orwell's books are lost on them -- and they just don't care. 

This should sound familiar. This game felt like a fluffy beach-read dystopia in 2016, but it quickly turned accurate once January 20th rolled around in 2017. Awesome.

It's a nice concept, specially if you like the surveillance theme. Orwell was able to explore the privacy problems that arise from an Orwellian society (many of them are already relevant today), with a nice and interesting story. However, the gameplay is very simple and not that interesting. Just some point and click actions on a PC screen, with lots of help from the game, so it doesn't really present a challenge. Worth playing it for the story and interesting theme.
I am now paranoid. great.

This is definitely worth a play through. Made me think long and hard about everything it supplied to me, and i honestly felt the weight of the characters - as if they were real people, even. An incredibly well-written game, that still has me thinking about it, even now.

I was overall satisfied with my purchase, The game isn't neccesary either pro or anti-surveillance, and the endings will allow you to come to your own conclusion as to whether a system like Orwell is worth it or not.
Intresting game, fun, and good price.

For the four and half hours I spent playing this game, I also occupied myself with watching television or movies. This is probably reasonably reflective of what I would do if I was one of these investigators in real life.

Orwell isn’t the most engaging of games in terms gameplay. It’s a simple task of continually dragging and dropping tidbits of information into the Orwell system so that it can compile the profiles and allow your “handler” to make assessments about the next course of engagement. Sometimes you have to choose between conflicting bits of information, but other than that, there’s generally little reason to not put information in the system as you come across it, except maybe to avoid your handler’s smart-arse remarks.

Orwell is a far more engaging game in terms of the ideas it presents and the world it builds. As I am sure you have guessed, Orwell derives heavily from the ideas put forward 1984 by George Orwell. Similarly to 1984, Orwell is set in a fictional country where media and many other outlets are controlled by the government. That being said, the Nation in which the game is set is more of an authoritarian society as opposed to full totalitarian.

By the time the ending rolled around, I was surprised by its direction. I mostly expected a “twist” where you are betrayed and would have to fight the government you were working for. But there was nothing quite that overt or direct, as you were presented with several opportunities with how to proceed. It was an interesting enough story built inside a world into which a lot of effort had been poured into its construction.

Orwell is not a thriller or a game that will keep you in suspense. Instead, it is a quiet and simple exploration of an old idea through a different lens, done tastefully and staying far enough away from the usual tropes to retain some uniqueness.
Veryyyy good story.
Fun game with an interesting storyline!

The great part of Orwell is that you're some kind of spy and see what everyone is doing, which helps you by solving the case. It's a great story and I really enjoyed it, though there are some cons. First, it's quite short; I finished it in 4/5 hours, it was worth it though. Second, the end of the story wasn't satisfying. It feels like the perpetrator just confessess, so to me it didn't feel like I solved it myself. At the beginning of the final chapter I really didn't have an idea who did it, but suddenly he/she just tells it him/herself. That wasn't satisfying, while the first four chapters were pretty awesome and exciting. I really hope there'll be another story or game like this, because it's very enjoyable; a must buy!

Very simple point and click game. If you enjoy online stalking, this is definitely your type of game ;) It's only a few hours of play, very simple but fun.

Likes; simple, point and click, quick gameplay, story rich, interesting characters, intriguing, mysterious, edge of your seat while the story twists and turns.

Dislikes; some of the answers are a bit guided, the first ending I got was a bummer and quick to end after a few quick choices made, it's not as 'free play' as I would have liked.
Brilliant. A chilling insight into how data collection via government surveillance can implicate an individual.

This is an incredible game! As a fan of "1984", the subtle references to the novel were a bonus, but that being said, you do not need to read the novel to play this game! It is incredible and I highly reccommend it to anyone who enjoys dystopian future, hacking, strategy games, or a game that is played entirely from the perspective of your own computer screen!

This is a fantastic game for those interested in interactive narrative. One of the most impressive elements of Orwell is its ability to challenge the player with choices where ethical dilemmas are implicit at every turn, with real consequences for your actions. Morality is inherent to the game's system, creating a wonderful sense of uncertainty throughout play. It also does an excellent job of outlining both sides in a realistic, balanced manner, with characters behaving in a nuanced way: well-meaning but flawed. Though there is no real action, and some might find the "read and upload" gameplay tedious, it uses clever mechanisms within the game's system to provide exciting real-time plot moments to break things up a bit.
This game was so intriguing and clever.  I've played through a few times and get so many different responses depending on the choices I've made.

NSA simulator. This game has a great story and a pretty good art style. The writing is on a whole different level, with plot twists and surprises. This is one of the few games that really feel like your choices make an impact on the game,

Really nice game.
Story is interesting, opposed to what I was worried could happen aften being blown away by Episode 1.
Game is also presented in really nice format - each episode takes around 45-60 minutes and it's nice to take a break for some thinking between them.
Experienced one bug during the whole playthrough, but even then I could continue from almost the same moment thanks to the autosave.
I'll definitely try to play it at least once more. :)

You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.
Just not a lot there.

Ok, so first off if you like the book, 1984, I think you'll enjoy this. This was one of my favourites of the last year purely for the concept. It's very interesting and story driven, but beware it doesn't take long to complete. Overall, I recommend this game.
Just Brilliant, Totally loved this game, but OMG it ended way too soon! What the hell am I going to obsess about now??????

Great Game!
I really enjoyed playing it very nice interface which is easy to understand.
Fun to follow developing story that adapts to you.
10/10

Orwell is one of the most engaging and realistic games I've every played. I never felt so conflicted over the information I was giving to the government! A beautifully designed game, I just wish it didn't have to end quietly so soon!

Hopefully, an addition to the game will be made soon! :D

If you like what Orwell is offering, it's worth a look. For the most part, it's a story. You play an investigator who has access to an amazing piece of spying technology. You immediately use it to help prevent a threat to The Nation. The "game" is played by viewing websites, texts, emails, and computers for information. When you find something incriminating, you upload it. The system then opens up other related sources for you to look through, and highlights the relevant data. It's up to you to upload it for further analysis or not.

Basically, you have to drag and drop the right highlighted text to Orwell in order to advance the story. It's not hard to do, and it keeps the story flowing nicely. It works, even if the ending is a bit rushed, and out of the blue.

This could have been more of a game if they didn't highlight the relevant data chunks, and actually had you select the right data. Later in the game, it actually limits how many data chunks you can upload. Again, this makes it more of a game. Still, that may not be to everyone's liking. Regardless, I played it with the same intensity as reading through an engaging novel. It's good for what it is. Play the demo and see if it's for you.
Very Good Game! I am looking forward to seeing more games from this publisher.

Short and simple.
It has a very enjoyible narrative where you play as a sort of detective.
Gameplay is limited by rules that are stated in the begining. 

Some more information?
The game is designed for the curious and detective types to search through forums, profiles, live text channels, and police reports to figure out who and why the cause of horrible events happen.
However you can also just as effectively "play" the game by scrolling through the pages only looking for the light-blue highlighted words to which you click and drag to the left on the profiles. For live chat rooms, you can just wait for information to show up that is able to be clicked on. The only time where you make a true decision is if you find yellow-highlighted text that contridicts information located somewhere else.

As a narrative experience for those who want to relax back and feel part of the story, this game is fantastic for you.
 For those who thought this would be a Challenging experience will be dissatisfied by simplistic gameplay of clicking and dragging.
seeing the world through the other side of the surveillance systems. if you like to read a lot and merge facts in a greater view.. here you go!
The game holds your hand a ridiculous amount. Waste of money.
DASHWOOD
Thoroughly enjoyed this game. A lot of twists and turns. Don't make assumptions because you WILL be wrong.

This is a difficult one! The premise and the story are both quite complicated and intelligently woven. However, the execution is less so. This game suffers from the very same type of problems that LA Noire did: how to make a detective/analysis game without too little or too much handholding.

The idea of the investigative software is quite well-written; and depending on your ending, has a lot of payoffs. But the fact that the software pinpoints what it thinks is important and relevant kinda breaks the realism and limits a lot of your options. A lot of times, decisions that you make won't have the intended consequences and not because "life is complicated" or "shit happens" but because that's now how you linguistically interpreted the data. And that is the limitation of every game that has attempted to use language as a mechanic. There are still too many unknowns and interpretations to be able to identify and script every possible `effect` after you've set a `cause`.


Of course, there's no undo or rollback so you have to keep going with what you've done so far. The concept of `conflicting info` is also weird and unrealistic. Sometimes, it warns you that this info conflicts with some other info that you haven't even loaded or read. How does the software know that?! I realize that this aspect of analysis needs to be "gamefied" but that's where this game shows its greatest weakness. It's as if the software is already run by an AI and you just need to answer a few multiple choice questions here and there.

There's also a number of annoying UI issues like notifications. I kept gettings notifications for new or unread articles when I had accessed them and read them numerous times. Same with the datachunk notification. And when you're hunting for something specific towards the end of the game, and you have a ton of data, those icons can get downright annoying and misleading forcing you to skim and scroll through heaps of useless articles.

Still, the game and the story have a lot to say about our current society and it's definitely worth a replay for things you might have missed the first time. Not to mention that it has multiple endings.

The music's quite good too!

This is a great game. In fact its an amazing game, the multiple endings and choices of what to do really make you feel a part of the peoples lives and their fates. The Story is great with a few clever twists and will keep you interested. The graphics are pretty good in my opinion, i like the artstyle it has, also the music in the background goes well with the game itself. However I feel the story could have een made longer but its good for its price tag. 

I rate the game a solid 8/10
Nothing to say. 10/10.

Cerebral brain that makes you think about the boundaries between prviacy, freedom, and security. 8-10 hour play through, but you'll want to play through again to see how the branching choices change the outcome for the characters. Conceptually interesting and feels realistic.

This game is pretty cool - you need to investigate people and try to prevent crimes! But then, the information you pass on can be interpretted so many ways... I was horrified when I got one person arrested and interrogated for torture. (if you do the same you'll know why!)

There's a powerful message in this game (surprise surprise!) and it's well delivered. I'm not obsessed with surveillance, but this makes a strong cause for caution when using "smart" and time saving technology, especially where human language is involved. The game isn't preachy though, and (I think) you have a choice, which makes it fun despite the scary/serious undertone.

The delivery is perfect - even though that means staring at a lot of that light blue screen, the whole thing is very immersive and feels like you're participatiung in something real.

As it stands now, I completed the story in 4.4 hours and don't think I'll be playing the game again.

Gameplay heavily revolves around story. For those who are not into reading a lot - this game will likely turn into a scroll, click, drag and drop simulator. 

With that out of the way - the story has problems. It seems to be a bit too linear and one-sided. With so much emphasis on the story and so much work and input I had to provide to move it forward I expected to be a bit more deeply surprised and moved throughout. The ending seemed a bit rushed and abrupt.

I look forward to checking the next title by this developer and I would pay more for a longer story of higher caliber with more twists and turns, with more varied gameplay and with some potential for replayability. 

I do commend the developer for attempting something new and for taking a stab at an important contemporary topic.

Thank you!
A great game and a great fear for ton of people ;)

Orwell. Is an awesome game, short but very full of detail. I was on my toes every second of this game, very well done. It had surprises and plot-twists everywhere. I highly recommend this game. I hope to see either a longer DLC or a new game that is like this. Very well done!  10/10 :D

I had a great time with this game. It took a topical issue and made an interesting narrative with a good cast of characters. The choices were at times very difficult with unclear consequences that made the morality of what you were doing even murkier. 
The mechanic where your supervisor only reports what you submit shows the real strength of this game- the writing. Symes can be misled very masterfully if you're careful about what you give him and when you do. Very appealing.
I just finished my second playthrough and will do a third to get the last of the achievements.

ONE MAJOR BUG - In Episode Five, when the supervisor would finish talking to you, the Orwell interface would still have the transparent blue overlay and wouldn't accept any clicks. This distrupted the flow of the finale significantly, forcing me to close and reopen the game. Happened five times over two playthroughs. Please fix

Besides other games near real-life graphics, immensely big worlds to explore or other ultra complex life simulators, its games like this that show the other side of the big potential computer games have for that thing called IMMERSION. 

And even if this statement could scare away some numb minded folks, games like this also show the potential to EDUCATE. Not in the sense of a boring lecture on morale but in the sense of a well written novel which makes you identify with the protagonists, feel with them and EXPERIENCE with them. 

I am well above my thirties and it is games like this that I want to shove in the face of people that still claim that computer games are childs stuff and cannot be serious and/or tackle real life issues while keeping me absolutely hooked for my playtime.

People with a short attention span in reading might get a hard time because there is a lot to read but like in every good piece of art (in the broad sense of movies, books etc.) you get the most out of those where you have to invest a little bit of yourself.

My suggestion:
If you've read my pseudo-academical review so far, do yourself (and the devs) a favor and play this game.

Fantastic game, and shockingly shows what might happen / or is happening right now with ever increasing surveillance. This game puts you in the place of an investigator scanning through the lifes of target persons. You experience first hand what consequences your investigations have - and what happens when you are not mindful about what information you pass on.

Very recommended. Be aware though that you need to read a lot.

amazing game, unlike anything else i've played. really good for people who love story and coming up with thories about what is going on. would like some extra info on the UI and some of the smaller details don't trigger perfectly, but i only really noticed this on my second play through. would also really like to have more control over my own character in the game, such as adding more details or past history that sort of thing.

I would very much like to see a sequel to this, though i'm not sure how that would fit in to the story.

As many others have mentioned, an interesting concept. Don't purchase this game looking for a good gameplay experience. This is certainly a visual novel with a little more interaction than usual, closing in on Point & Click Adventure territory.

It certainly has its own contemporary agenda, which they do a fairly good job at conveying. Its execution isn't always the best, some moments fall flat but are remedied by the pacing and -for me, personally- the desire to see what is going to happen next. While short, it offers enough of interest to be worth a purchase (perhaps at a 40-50% discount, depending on your tastes). 

The 'choices' you will encounter in this game usually boil down to 'jump to conclusion' and 'don't jump to conclusion', which can admittedly work out well in some cases. However, there are times where you will encounter unforseen consequences. These can definitely have an impact on how the game progresses, in increments. For the most part you are playing through a story on rails, with only a few forks in the road that eventually lead to the same place, anyways. The biggest choice you will get takes place at the end of the game, where you will most likely arrive after about 4 hours. 

I would say the game is worth playing for its subject matter alone, it stands on its own as an experience. Some food for thought is to be found, as well.

Few games manage to solve the equation to be interesting, involving, and fun. Orwell is such a game. While it provides a biased view on the topic of surveillance (a view I wholeheartedly approve of, incidentally), it manages to stay informative. The possibles misuses made by the "Orwell" tool you are in control of clearly address the old myth that yes, contrary to what your grandparents say, everybody does have something to hide.

The game portrays a situation where nothing is ever white or black. Even the all-spying government you work for seem to have good intents. Orwell does not try to tell you that you live in a secret dictatorship, instead, it describes perfectly the mechanic of how a tool, a system can be used, abused by a soulless entity to draw wrong conclusions and to make void of the old concept of "private life".

As a game, and that means I will address gameplay here, Orwell partially fails. The game seems to imply that the things you decide to add to the Orwell database have all to be relevant else there is going to be some serious consequences : during my one and only playthrough, however, it felt like I was on rail and that I could not fail anything. Only in the final episode of the game choices I made during that episode seemed to matter, and I am not even sure to which extent (besides the choice of endings). If you are looking for a game of strategy, this is not your game.

If, however, you are looking for either a compelling story, an education on how your Internet activity can tell all about you, proof that the concept of serious games is not a futility, or an interesting twist on the old detectove point&click adventure genre, Orwell is definitely your game. It's a Snowden's Paper Please.

All you do is drag and drop little snippets of information, that is it. I would not even call this a game to be honest. Drag and drop, that is all there is to it.

Would i recommend this drag and drop simulation: No, not even if it was free.

Still yet to see where the choices are, which apparently matter. Had one at the end, investigate Gov or Hacker, but still ends the same. How did that choice matter?

This game f*cked with my mind. Oh heavenly gods of nerddom, did it ever. Gather round, boys and girls, as I tell you why:

Orwell takes place in a country called "The Nation" (obviously not to be confused with anything casually tyrannical like "The Empire"). The political ruling party, The Party (much imaginative), has come into power and, thanks to the newly created office of the Secretary of Security, has in the last few years passed a Safety Bill meant to protect The Nation from any and every individual(s) who pose a threat to national security (think of the Patriot Act as a IRL equivalent). And just like NSA wiretapping, the Safety Bill gives the government dubious leeway to monitor suspected individuals through various channels (i.e., social media, email, phone calls, text messages, etc). The computer program the government employs to collect and complie such information is ironically named "Orwell" and you are hired as an Orwell investigator to track down a group of suspected individuals believed to be responsible for a series of bombings that have occurred in The Nation's capitol city of Bonton (ridiculous name I have to say, I couldn't stop thinking of bonbons). As an investigator you are paired with an adviser through whom you pass information on to higher channels who take the appropriate action. Although you are given objectives whose completion is information-dependent, it becomes ultimately clear that you, the investigator, your judgement, your discerning eye, your evaluation of possible repercussions of all the information at your fingertips, is what drives the game. The endgame of Orwell depends on you and your choices. Will you do the right thing, whatever you believe is the right thing? 

Aesthetics-wise, this game is just pretty damn near pleasing. It's a simple point-and-click with elegant yet simple graphics. The attention to detail is great, from the texts to the functionality of Orwell itself. The whole feel of the game, especially at certain moments (I'm not going to be a no-good, spoiley spoilsport), makes one forget that this is JUST A SIMULATION, NOT REAL LIFE CALM THE F*CK DOWN. I will say it's easy to get overwhelmed by the sheer density of information and how to appropriately navigate, in terms of the expected outcome. But hey, maybe it's a personal thing. I am more used to FPS than this sort of genre of game. 

In conclusion: PLAY THE GAME, FAM. DO IT. JUST DO IT!

I bought this game because of all the good reviews, and while the game was enticing at certain times, and it had a great premise; it's literally only 5 hours worth of gameplay and that's it. There isn't even a repetive mode like in Papers, Please where you can at least mess around in the game outside of the story. There's no sub-quests, or sub-stories. There's nothing but the very short main story and CREDITS "THANKS FOR PLAYING". The ending is very unrewarding as well.

If this game were a few bucks, I wouldn't have complained; but $10+ depending on when you bought it? I guess it's better than going to the movies (in some ways), but I was left very unfulfilled by this. If all 5 of those hours were gripping and suspenseful like the few moments in this game that were? It'd have been worth it, but it doesn't quite succeed at that.

TL;DR: Not a bad game, but only one storyline, no sub-plots, no game to be done outside of the main story. Main story is also waaaay too fast. Also not much diversity in storyline no matter what you choose/do. You are pretty much just walked through the entire storyline the whole game.

Compelling. Immersive. Intense. Orwell is all of these things as it shows us the future of online privacy (increasingly an oxymoron in this age) and how easy it is/will be to curtail our civil liberties, even with only the best of intentions.

Much like Papers, Please, this game gives you an unpopular (to say the least) but reasonably straightforward job. Soon, however, you discover just how crucial your decisions are - and how dire the consequences can be. Of course, you are simply doing your job; you're not a [i]villain[/i]... but, looking at your actions, are you distinguishable from one?

Orwell is a game that touches on many important topics, including but not limited to...

- privacy, both as a basic societal concept and as a political issue
- the importance of context (and the dangers of losing/removing it)
- whether the ends justify the means (openness to truth versus confirmation bias/cherrypicking)
- the importance of critical reading (instead of passive credulity)
- identity, which can be variously represented as one's experiences and/or past actions and/or speech (and the pitfalls of giving any one instance too much weight)
- idealism and its potential for corruption
- law as a power unto itself

I enjoyed and [b]recommend[/b] this game for its well-paced character-driven story, effective mood-setting music, and overall attractive presentation.

[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

Still, this is an excellent game with excellent graphics and a pretty deep storyline too. 10/10

Probably the most aggrivating thing about this game is the inability to directly say what information you extract should mean. Instead you effectively hand over little quips of information to a conspiricy theorist and then wonder how that information is going to be used. Probably the biggest instance of this is when you are going to arrest a certain character, you get into a certain call. You learn that she is on the move, and has a hand gun. You submit that she has a gun and suddenly you basicaly called the fekin army down on her and she dies, when all evidence before then would suggest that going Riot-shields fer days would have been the correct move.

Also when handed "Contradicting evidence", often times the information isn't contradicting, but should have been able to be combined to paint something that would have been more conductive to profiling the person in question. Things like where the suspect lives now and previously, which both could be noted and later on used to help track down said person.

The lack of proper notes is, while not entirely nessisary for the set up of the game, probably a bad decision. Notes could have been used to snip articles with evidence that your unsure of how to use at the present moment and would have helped during the "Scrolling sections" disguised as Texts and calls. While you can scroll up during any moment of these, being able to hold out on certain information for a better time would have helped immensely.

So all in all, a great premise and the story works, execution worked about as well as alcohol and fire.

The premise is simple:  you are an investigator for Orwell, a government surveillance network for a fictious country called The Nation. You are tasked with investigated people who might be involved with a series of government bombings. 

It is a game that spans five episodes, and I finished in in about seven hours, so the game doesn't have much in the way of replayability, unless you're looking to see how else the game ends (it has the potential of three separate endings). Even though it lacks in replayability, it's an interesting and complex game that's definitely worth giving a try .
